question: Is the Son of God true God from true God, begotten not made, consubstantial with the Father?
catholic_answer: Yes. The Son is true God from true God, begotten not made, of one substance with the Father, through whom all things were made.
breakaway_answer: No. The Son is not of one substance with the Father. He is a created being—or otherwise not true God in the same sense as the Father—and is subordinate to him.
passage_excerpt: We believe in one God, the Father Almighty, maker of all things visible and invisible; and in one Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, the only-begotten of his Father, of the substance of the Father, God of God, Light of Light, very God of very God, begotten (γεννηθέντα), not made, being of one substance (ὁμοούσιον, consubstantialem) with the Father. By whom all things were made, both which be in heaven and in earth. Who for us men and for our salvation came down [from heaven] and was incarnate…

question: Must Melitian clergy be received only under the Alexandrian settlement that strips Meletius of authority and places succession under the bishop of Alexandria’s ratification?
catholic_answer: Yes. Melitian clergy may be received under the synod’s terms, but Meletius himself is granted no authority or privilege; succession among those received requires the people’s election and the bishop of Alexandria’s concurrence.
breakaway_answer: No. The parallel hierarchy and Meletius’s claims are not extinguished under that Alexandrian settlement; the schism’s episcopal legitimacy is not surrendered on those terms.
canonical_citation: Nicaea I Synodal Letter to the Church of Alexandria
passage_excerpt: To the Church of Alexandria, by the grace of God, holy and great; and to our well-beloved brethren, the orthodox clergy and laity throughout Egypt, and Pentapolis, and Lybia, and every nation under heaven, the holy and great synod, the bishops assembled at Nicea, wish health in the Lord. Forasmuch as the great and holy Synod, which was assembled at Niece through the grace of Christ and our most religious Sovereign Constantine, who brought us together from our several provinces and cities, has…

question: If bishops subscribe Nestorius’s deposition and then reverse course, are they to be treated as having joined apostasy from Ephesus’s judgment?
catholic_answer: Yes. Bishops who reverse after subscribing that deposition have joined apostasy and are to be removed from the priesthood; the deposition stands as binding orthodoxy.
breakaway_answer: No. That deposition is not binding orthodoxy. Communion may continue without treating reversal of subscription as apostasy from the faith.
passage_excerpt: If any provincial bishops were not present at the holy Synod and have joined or attempted to join the apostacy; or if, after subscribing the deposition of Nestorius, they went back into the assembly of apostates; these men, according to the decree of the holy Synod, are to be deposed from the priesthood and degraded from their rank.

question: Is it unlawful to compose or introduce a creed different from the faith of Nicaea as received by the Council of Ephesus?
catholic_answer: Yes. It is unlawful to compose or introduce a creed different from the faith already established by the fathers in the Holy Spirit; that creed alone settles the faith for reception.
breakaway_answer: No. That ban is not authoritative. The faith may be confessed in a different settlement that distinguishes divinity and humanity more sharply than that synod required.
passage_excerpt: When these things had been read, the holy Synod decreed that it is unlawful for any man to bring forward, or to write, or to compose a different (ἑτέραν) Faith as a rival to that established by the holy Fathers assembled with the Holy Ghost in Nicæa. But those who shall dare to compose a different faith, or to introduce or offer it to persons desiring to turn to the acknowledgment of the truth, whether from Heathenism or from Judaism, or from any heresy whatsoever, shall be deposed, if they be…

question: Is the Emmanuel very God, and is the Holy Virgin therefore Mother of God (Theotokos) because she bore the Word of God made flesh?
catholic_answer: Yes. The Emmanuel is very God, and the Holy Virgin is Mother of God inasmuch as she bore the Word made flesh.
breakaway_answer: No—not under that forced Theotokos settlement. She is confessed as Mother of Christ; divinity and humanity remain sharply distinguished as two qnome.
passage_excerpt: If anyone will not confess that the Emmanuel is very God, and that therefore the Holy Virgin is the Mother of God (Θεοτόκος), inasmuch as in the flesh she bore the Word of God made flesh [as it is written, The Word was made flesh] let him be anathema.

question: Is our Great High Priest the divine Word made flesh himself, or another man distinct from the Word?
catholic_answer: The divine Word made flesh himself is our Great High Priest and Apostle. There is not another man, distinct from the Word, who offers sacrifice for us.
breakaway_answer: Not as a forced identity of the high priest with the Word alone. The high-priestly work is confessed in the humanity as distinct from the divinity (two qnome), without collapsing them into one subject in that way.
passage_excerpt: Whosoever shall say that it is not the divine Word himself, when he was made flesh and had become man as we are, but another than he, a man born of a woman, yet different from him (ἰδικῶς ἄνθρωπον), who has become our Great High Priest and Apostle; or if any man shall say that he offered himself in sacrifice for himself and not rather for us, whereas, being without sin, he had no need of offering or sacrifice: let him be anathema.

question: Does the flesh of the Lord give life because it is the Word’s own flesh?
catholic_answer: Yes. The Lord’s flesh gives life because it is the Word’s own flesh, belonging to him as his very own.
breakaway_answer: No—not under that forced wording. The flesh may be life-giving, yet divinity and humanity remain sharply distinct qnome rather than one flesh that is simply ‘the Word’s own’ in that sense.
passage_excerpt: Whosoever shall not confess that the flesh of the Lord gives life and that it pertains to the Word of God the Father as his very own, but shall pretend that it belongs to another person who is united to him [i.e., the Word] only according to honour, and who has served as a dwelling for the divinity; and shall not rather confess, as we say, that that flesh gives life because it is that of the Word who gives life to all: let him be anathema.

question: Did the Word of God suffer, get crucified, and taste death in the flesh?
catholic_answer: Yes. The Word of God suffered, was crucified, and tasted death in the flesh—those passions are truly said of the Word in his flesh.
breakaway_answer: No—not in that sense. The Word’s divinity remains impassible; suffering, crucifixion, and death belong to the humanity distinctly, not to the divine nature.
passage_excerpt: Whosoever shall not recognize that the Word of God suffered in the flesh, that he was crucified in the flesh, and that likewise in that same flesh he tasted death and that he has become the first-begotten of the dead, for, as he is God, he is the life and it is he that gives life: let him be anathema.

question: After the hypostatic union, may one divide the hypostases in the one Christ as joined only by worthiness or authority rather than by natural union?
catholic_answer: No. After the hypostatic union one may not divide the hypostases as joined only by worthiness or authority. The union is a real, natural coming-together in one Christ.
breakaway_answer: Yes, in this sense: divinity and humanity remain two qnome sharply distinguished. Their connection is not that ‘natural union’ which would erase the dual integrity of the natures.
passage_excerpt: If anyone shall after the [hypostatic] union divide the hypostases in the one Christ, joining them by that connection alone, which happens according to worthiness, or even authority and power, and not rather by a coming together (συνόδῳ), which is made by natural union (ἕνωσιν φυσικὴν): let him be anathema.

question: May scriptural sayings about Christ be divided between two persons—some to a man apart from the Word, others only to the Word as God?
catholic_answer: No. Scriptural sayings about Christ must not be split between two persons—some applied only to a man apart from the Word, others only to the Word as God. They are said of the one Christ.
breakaway_answer: Yes, in a careful dyophysite assignment: some sayings belong to the humanity, others to the divinity, because the two qnome are not collapsed into one subject of attribution.
passage_excerpt: If anyone shall divide between two persons or subsistences those expressions (φωνάς) which are contained in the Evangelical and Apostolical writings, or which have been said concerning Christ by the Saints, or by himself, and shall apply some to him as to a man separate from the Word of God, and shall apply others to the only Word of God the Father, on the ground that they are fit to be applied to God: let him be anathema.

question: Is the assumed man to be worshipped together with the Word as two different things, or is Emmanuel worshipped with one adoration?
catholic_answer: Emmanuel is worshipped with one adoration. The assumed man is not worshipped together with the Word as two different things side by side.
breakaway_answer: Worship may honor the distinction of the two qnome. A single ‘one adoration’ that forbids any dual reference is not required; the humanity is not absorbed into an undifferentiated cult of the Word alone.
passage_excerpt: If anyone shall dare to say that the assumed man (ἀναληφθέντα) ought to be worshipped together with God the Word, and glorified together with him, and recognised together with him as God, and yet as two different things, the one with the other (for this Together with is added [i.e., by the Nestorians] to convey this meaning); and shall not rather with one adoration worship the Emmanuel and pay to him one glorification, as [it is written] The Word was made flesh: let him be anathema.

question: Was the one Lord Jesus Christ glorified by the Holy Spirit as using a power not his own, or as his own Spirit working miracles?
catholic_answer: He was glorified by his own Spirit working miracles—not by using a power foreign to himself.
breakaway_answer: Not under that forced alternative. The Spirit’s wonders in Christ are confessed while keeping the distinction of divinity and humanity, without accepting that exclusive wording.
passage_excerpt: If any man shall say that the one Lord Jesus Christ was glorified by the Holy Ghost, so that he used through him a power not his own and from him received power against unclean spirits and power to work miracles before men and shall not rather confess that it was his own Spirit through which he worked these divine signs; let him be anathema.

question: Is the Holy Virgin rightly called Mother of God (Theotokos) because the Word united to flesh is one Christ and one Son from two natures in true union?
catholic_answer: Yes. The Holy Virgin is rightly called Mother of God, because the Word united to flesh is one Christ and one Son from two natures in true union—not because the Godhead began from her.
breakaway_answer: No. The preferred title is Mother of Christ. Mother of God is not required; it risks confusing the natures if taken as that settlement enforced it.
canonical_citation: Ephesus, Epistle of Cyril to Nestorius (Intelligo quosdam)
passage_excerpt: To the most religious and beloved of God, fellow minister Nestorius, Cyril sends greeting in the Lord. I hear that some are rashly talking of the estimation in which I hold your holiness, and that this is frequently the case especially at the times that meetings are held of those in authority. And perchance they think in so doing to say something agreeable to you, but they speak senselessly, for they have suffered no injustice at my hands, but have been exposed by me only to their profit; this…

question: Must the letter said to be of Ibas to Maris—denying that the Word was made man of Mary Mother of God and attacking Cyril and Ephesus—be rejected rather than defended?
catholic_answer: Yes. That letter is to be rejected, not defended; its denial of the Word made man of Mary Mother of God and its attack on Cyril and Ephesus are condemned.
breakaway_answer: No. That letter’s sharper distinction of divinity and humanity may be defended; the Cyrilline anathematizing settlement is not accepted as binding in that way.
passage_excerpt: If anyone shall defend that letter which Ibas is said to have written to Maris the Persian, in which he denies that the Word of God incarnate of Mary, the Holy Mother of God and ever-virgin, was made man, but says that a mere man was born of her, whom he styles a Temple, as though the Word of God was one Person and the man another person; in which letter also he reprehends St. Cyril as a heretic, when he teaches the right faith of Christians, and charges him with writing things like to the…

question: Is the ever-virgin Mary exactly and truly the Mother of God, because God the Word was made flesh and born of her?
catholic_answer: Yes. She is exactly and truly the Mother of God, because God the Word begotten of the Father was in these last days made flesh and born of her.
breakaway_answer: No—not as that forced ‘exactly and truly’ Theotokos confession. Mother of Christ language is preferred, keeping divinity and humanity distinct.
passage_excerpt: If anyone shall not call in a true acceptation, but only in a false acceptation, the holy, glorious, and ever-virgin Mary, the Mother of God, or shall call her so only in a relative sense, believing that she bare only a simple man and that God the word was not incarnate of her, but that the incarnation of God the Word resulted only from the fact that he united himself to that man who was born [of her]; if he shall calumniate the Holy Synod of Chalcedon as though it had asserted the Virgin to…

question: After the Incarnation, is Jesus Christ to be confessed in two natures, without confusion, change, division, or separation, united in one person and one hypostasis?
catholic_answer: Yes. After the Incarnation, the one and the same Son is confessed in two natures, without confusion, change, division, or separation, the property of each preserved in one person and one hypostasis.
breakaway_answer: No. After the union he is confessed as one united nature of the Word incarnate (miaphysite)—perfect in divinity and humanity without separating them into two natures after the union.
passage_excerpt: The holy, great, and ecumenical synod, assembled by the grace of God and the command of our most religious and Christian Emperors, Marcian and Valentinian, Augusti, at Chalcedon, the metropolis of the Bithynian Province, in the martyry of the holy and victorious martyr Euphemia, has decreed as follows: Our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, when strengthening the knowledge of the Faith in his disciples, to the end that no one might disagree with his neighbour concerning the doctrines of religion,…

question: When Chalcedon speaks of one person/hypostasis of Christ, does that mean a Nestorian union of many hypostases, or the Word united to flesh in one hypostasis?
catholic_answer: It means the Word united to flesh in one hypostasis. It does not mean a mere union of many hypostases under one honorary ‘person.’
breakaway_answer: That ‘one person’ language is not received in their sense. One united nature of the Word incarnate is confessed, without endorsing their gloss on that formula.
passage_excerpt: If anyone understands the expression one only Person of our Lord Jesus Christ in this sense, that it is the union of many hypostases, and if he attempts thus to introduce into the mystery of Christ two hypostases, or two Persons, and, after having introduced two persons, speaks of one Person only out of dignity, honour or worship, as both Theodorus and Nestorius insanely have written; if anyone shall calumniate the holy Council of Chalcedon, pretending that it made use of this expression [one…

question: When we say Christ is in two natures, do we mean an unconfused hypostatic union in which each nature remains what it was?
catholic_answer: Yes. ‘In two natures’ names the unconfused hypostatic union in which divinity and humanity each remain what they were in the one Lord Jesus Christ.
breakaway_answer: No. That ‘in two natures’ settlement is refused; after the union he is confessed as one united nature of the Word incarnate.
passage_excerpt: If anyone using the expression, in two natures, does not confess that our one Lord Jesus Christ has been revealed in the divinity and in the humanity, so as to designate by that expression a difference of the natures of which an ineffable union is unconfusedly made, [a union] in which neither the nature of the Word was changed into that of the flesh, nor that of the flesh into that of the Word, for each remained that it was by nature, the union being hypostatic; but shall take the expression…

question: Does confessing two natures—or the one nature of God the Word made flesh—mean a hypostatic union of Godhead and humanity in one Christ without mixture or confusion?
catholic_answer: Yes. Either expression, rightly used, means the hypostatic union of Godhead and humanity in one Christ without mixture or confusion of the natures.
breakaway_answer: No. The binding reception of that regulation of the phrases is refused; after the union he is confessed as one united nature of the Word incarnate.
passage_excerpt: If anyone uses the expression of two natures, confessing that a union was made of the Godhead and of the humanity, or the expression the one nature made flesh of God the Word, and shall not so understand those expressions as the holy Fathers have taught, to wit: that of the divine and human nature there was made an hypostatic union, whereof is one Christ; but from these expressions shall try to introduce one nature or substance [made by a mixture] of the Godhead and manhood of Christ; let him…

question: Must the Constantinopolitan creed be sung with the Filioque, and must Chalcedon’s two natures and the sixth council’s two wills be accepted?
catholic_answer: Yes. The creed is to be received with ‘and the Son,’ and Chalcedon’s two natures in one person and the sixth council’s two wills are to be accepted.
breakaway_answer: No. The Filioque addition is refused, and Christ is confessed in the miaphysite settlement rather than under those two-natures and two-wills union terms.
passage_excerpt: The following is contained in it. First, you give to our people of the Armenians the holy creed of Constantinople, with the added phrase and the Son, to be sung or read within the mass in our churches at least on Sundays and greater feasts. Secondly, the definition of the fourth universal council of Chalcedon about two natures in the one person of Christ.

question: Did Chalcedon and Pope Leo rightly define the truth about two natures in Christ?
catholic_answer: Yes. That synod and that pope rightly defined the truth about two natures in the one person of Christ.
breakaway_answer: No. They did not rightly define that truth. After the union there is one united nature of the Word incarnate, not two natures as they taught.
passage_excerpt: Fourthly, you declare that the synod of Chalcedon and most blessed pope Leo rightly defined the truth about two natures in the one person of Christ against the impious doctrines of Nestorius and Eutyches. You order that we should venerate most blessed Leo as holy and a pillar of the faith and that we should reverently accept not only the synods of Nicaea, Constantinople and the first of Ephesus, but also all other synods legitimately celebrated . .

question: In the sacrifice of the altar, must a little water be mixed with the wine in the chalice?
catholic_answer: Yes. While the chalice is offered, a little water is to be mixed with the wine.
breakaway_answer: No. The wine is offered unmixed; mixing water with the wine at the altar is not required.
passage_excerpt: Fifthly, a short scheme of the seven sacraments of the church, namely baptism, confirmation, Eucharist, penance, extreme unction, orders and matrimony indicating the matter, the form and the minister of each; and that while the chalice is being offered in the sacrifice of the altar a little water should be mixed with the wine.

question: Does the Holy Spirit proceed from the Father and the Son, are the penitent cleansed after death by purifying pains, and does the Roman pontiff hold primacy over the whole Church?
catholic_answer: Yes. The Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son; the penitent may be cleansed after death by purifying pains; and the Roman pontiff holds primacy over the whole Church.
breakaway_answer: No. The Spirit proceeds from the Father; that purgatory formulation of purifying pains is not received; and Roman universal primacy is refused.
passage_excerpt: Seventhly, the decree of union concluded with the Greeks, which was promulgated earlier in this sacred council, recording how the holy Spirit proceeds eternally from the Father and the Son, and that the phrase and the Son was licitly and reasonably added to the creed of Constantinople. Also that the body of the Lord is effected in leavened or unleavened wheat bread; and what is to be believed about the pains of purgatory and hell, about the life of the blessed and about suffrages offered for…

question: Must the Constantinopolitan creed be received with the added phrase 'and the Son' (Filioque) and used in the Armenian churches as Florence decrees?
catholic_answer: Yes. The creed must be received with the added phrase ‘and the Son,’ as a licit clarification of the truth, and used in the liturgy as decreed.
breakaway_answer: No. The creed must stand without that added phrase. Requiring ‘and the Son’ as a condition of communion is rejected; procession is confessed from the Father.
passage_excerpt: In the first place, then, we give them the holy creed issued by the hundred and fifty bishops in the ecumenical council of Constantinople, with the added phrase and the Son, which for the sake of declaring the truth and from urgent necessity was licitly and reasonably added to that creed, which runs as follows: I believe . . .

question: Must the Armenians (and those entering Latin union) accept Chalcedon’s definition of two natures in the one person of Christ?
catholic_answer: Yes. Those entering union must accept the definition of two natures in the one person of Christ as the faith of the universal synods.
breakaway_answer: No. That two-nature definition is not the price of communion. The faith is the miaphysite confession of one united nature of the Word incarnate.
passage_excerpt: In the second place, we give them the definition of the fourth council of Chalcedon about two natures in the one person of Christ, which was later renewed in the fifth and sixth universal councils. It runs as follows: This wise and saving creed … Thirdly, the definition about the two wills and two principles of action of Christ promulgated in the above-mentioned sixth council, the tenor of which is This pious and orthodox creed, and the rest which follows in the above-mentioned definition of…

question: Must the Armenians accept Chalcedon and Pope Leo, contrary to the claim that both taught Nestorius’s heresy?
catholic_answer: Yes. They must accept that later synod and that pope. The claim that both taught the condemned dyophysite heresy is false; their definition is orthodox.
breakaway_answer: No. They are not to be accepted on those terms. The charge that they teach heresy is not settled by submitting to them; the miaphysite confession stands without that acceptance.
passage_excerpt: Fourth, apart from the three synods of Nicaea, Constantinople and the first of Ephesus, the Armenians have accepted no other later universal synods nor the most blessed Leo, bishop of this holy see, by whose authority the council of Chalcedon met. For they claim that it was proposed to them that both the synod of Chalcedon and the said Leo had made the definition in accordance with the condemned heresy of Nestorius. So we instructed them and declared that such a suggestion was false and that…

question: Can anyone outside the Catholic Church—pagans, Jews, heretics, or schismatics—share eternal life unless joined to that Church before death?
catholic_answer: No. Those outside the Church—pagans, Jews, heretics, or schismatics—cannot share eternal life unless joined to it before death. Only those who abide in that unity share the Church’s sacraments unto salvation.
breakaway_answer: Yes, eternal life is not closed to everyone outside that Latin communion. Salvation is found in the older Eastern church of the fathers; joining that Roman-defined body is not the condition of eternal life.
passage_excerpt: It firmly believes, professes and preaches that all those who are outside the catholic church, not only pagans but also Jews or heretics and schismatics, cannot share in eternal life and will go into the everlasting fire which was prepared for the devil and his angels, unless they are joined to the catholic church before the end of their lives; that the unity of the ecclesiastical body is of such importance that only for those who abide in it do the church’s sacraments contribute to salvation…

question: Should the second synod of Ephesus be condemned as impious for approving Eutychian error under Dioscorus?
catholic_answer: Yes. That second synod should be condemned as impious for approving Eutychian error under its Alexandrian president, who defended that heresy and persecuted the orthodox bishop of Constantinople.
breakaway_answer: No. That synod and its president are not to be condemned as impious Eutychian partisans. The president is remembered as a defender of orthodoxy against a wrong settlement, not as a heresiarch’s champion.
passage_excerpt: But it condemns, anathematizes and rejects the impious second synod of Ephesus, which was convened under our predecessor most blessed Leo and the aforesaid emperor. In it Dioscorus, bishop of Alexandria, defender of the heresiarch Eutyches and impious persecutor of holy Flavian, bishop of Constantinople, with cunning and threat led the execrable synod to an approval of the Eutychian impiety.

question: Must Christians embrace the Council of Chalcedon (630 fathers) as a universal council of the Church?
catholic_answer: Yes. Christians must embrace that council of the 630 fathers as a universal council of the Church, fourth among the ecumenical synods.
breakaway_answer: No. It is not a universal council of the Church. The binding christological settlement is the earlier miaphysite confession, not that two-nature definition.
passage_excerpt: It also embraces, approves and accepts the holy synod of 630 fathers at Chalcedon, which is fourth in the order of universal synods and was held in the time of our predecessor most blessed Leo and the emperor Marcian. In it the Eutychian heresy and its author Eutyches and its defender Dioscorus were condemned, and there was defined that our lord Jesus Christ is true God and true man and that in the one and same person the divine and human natures remain entire, inviolate, incorrupt, unconfused…

question: Must Christians accept Constantinople II, which renewed Chalcedon’s definition of two natures in one person of Christ?
catholic_answer: Yes. Christians must accept that fifth synod, including its renewal of the two-nature definition in one person of Christ and its condemnation of Origenist errors.
breakaway_answer: No. That synod is not accepted insofar as it renews the two-nature definition as binding. Orthodoxy is confessed in the miaphysite tradition without that renewal.
passage_excerpt: It also embraces, approves and accepts the fifth holy synod, the second of Constantinople, which was held in the time of our predecessor most blessed Vigilius and the emperor Justinian. In it the definition of the sacred council of Chalcedon about the two natures and the one person of Christ was renewed and many errors of Origen and his followers, especially about the penitence and liberation of demons and other condemned beings, were refuted and condemned.

question: Must Christians accept Constantinople III’s definition that in Christ there are two natures, two principles of action, and two wills in one person?
catholic_answer: Yes. In Christ there are two perfect natures, two principles of action, and two wills, in one and the same person.
breakaway_answer: No. That dyothelete / two-natures package is not required for communion. Christ is confessed in the miaphysite tradition without accepting those dualities as the binding settlement.
passage_excerpt: It also embraces, approves and accepts the third holy synod of 150 fathers at Constantinople, which is sixth in the order of universal synods and was convened in the time of our predecessor most blessed Agatho and the emperor Constantine IV. In it the heresy of Macarius of Antioch and his adherents was condemned, and there was defined that in our lord Jesus Christ there are two perfect and complete natures and two principles of action and also two wills, although there is one and the same…

question: Are universal synods those legitimately confirmed by the authority of a Roman pontiff, including Florence’s unions with the Greeks and Armenians?
catholic_answer: Yes. Universal synods are those legitimately confirmed by the Roman pontiff’s authority, including the recent unions and their definitions.
breakaway_answer: No. Universal synods are not defined by papal confirmation. Authority rests in the consensus of the ancient churches; those unions are not binding conditions of the faith.
passage_excerpt: It also embraces, approves and accepts all other universal synods which were legitimately summoned, celebrated and confirmed by the authority of a Roman pontiff, and especially this holy synod of Florence, in which, among other things, most holy unions with the Greeks and the Armenians have been achieved and many most salutary definitions in respect of each of these unions have been issued, as is contained in full in the decrees previously promulgated, which are as follows: Let the heavens be…

question: May fourth and further marriages be lawfully contracted when no canonical impediment exists?
catholic_answer: Yes. When no canonical impediment exists, not only second and third but also fourth and further marriages may lawfully be contracted.
breakaway_answer: No. Repeated remarriage is restricted; fourth and further marriages are not treated as freely lawful in that way.
passage_excerpt: It is asserted that some people reject fourth marriages as condemned. Lest sin is attributed where it does not exist, since the apostle says that a wife on her husband’s death is free from his law and free in the Lord to marry whom she wishes, and since no distinction is made between the deaths of the first, second and third husbands, we declare that not only second and third marriages but also fourth and further ones may lawfully be contracted, provided there is no canonical impediment. We…

question: Does the Holy Spirit proceed from the Father and the Son, as the holy Roman church professes in its teaching on the Trinity?
catholic_answer: Yes. The Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son: one God in three persons, the Spirit having his being from both.
breakaway_answer: No. The Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father. Procession ‘from the Father and the Son’ as from one principle is not confessed.
passage_excerpt: First, then, the holy Roman church, founded on the words of our Lord and Saviour, firmly believes, professes and preaches one true God, almighty, immutable and eternal, Father, Son and holy Spirit; one in essence, three in persons; unbegotten Father, Son begotten from the Father, holy Spirit proceeding from the Father and the Son; the Father is not the Son or the holy Spirit, the Son is not the Father or the holy Spirit, the holy Spirit is not the Father or the Son; the Father is only the…

question: Is one and the same Son perfect in divinity and humanity, true God and true man, acknowledged in two natures without confusion, change, division, or separation?
catholic_answer: Yes. One and the same Son is perfect in divinity and humanity, acknowledged in two natures without confusion, change, division, or separation.
breakaway_answer: No. After the union he is confessed as one united nature of the Word incarnate, not ‘in two natures’ as that definition requires.
passage_excerpt: Also it holds, professes and teaches that one and the same Son of God and of man, our lord Jesus Christ, is perfect in divinity and perfect in humanity; true God and true man, of a rational soul and a body; consubstantial with the Father as regards his divinity, consubstantial with us as regards his humanity; like us in all respects except for sin; begotten before the ages from the Father, and in the last days the same born according to his humanity for us and our salvation from Mary the…

question: Is Christ’s body truly confected in both unleavened and leavened bread, and are souls who die penitent but without full satisfaction cleansed after death by cleansing pains, aided by the Church’s suffrages?
catholic_answer: Yes on both counts. Christ’s body is truly confected in either unleavened or leavened wheat bread according to each church’s rite; and penitent souls who die without full satisfaction are cleansed after death by cleansing pains, helped by the suffrages of the living.
breakaway_answer: No on purgatorial cleansing pains and those Mass-centered suffrages as defined—the dead are prayed for, but not under that doctrine. Unleavened bread also remains contested; leavened bread is the proper use in the Eastern rite.
passage_excerpt: Also, the body of Christ is truly confected in both unleavened and leavened wheat bread, and priests should confect the body of Christ in either, that is, each priest according to the custom of his western or eastern church. Also, if truly penitent people die in the love of God before they have made satisfaction for acts and omissions by worthy fruits of repentance, their souls are cleansed after death by cleansing pains; and the suffrages of the living faithful avail them in giving relief…

question: Do souls free of sin (or cleansed of it) go straight to the beatific vision, while those dying in mortal or original sin alone go straight to hell?
catholic_answer: Yes. Purified souls go straight to the beatific vision, graded by merits; those dying in mortal sin or original sin alone go straight to hell, with unequal pains.
breakaway_answer: Not under that immediate heaven-or-hell schema as defined. The destiny of souls after death is confessed with prayer for the dead, without accepting that Latin mapping of destinies.
passage_excerpt: Also, the souls of those who have incurred no stain of sin whatsoever after baptism, as well as souls who after incurring the stain of sin have been cleansed whether in their bodies or outside their bodies, as was stated above, are straightaway received into heaven and clearly behold the triune God as he is, yet one person more perfectly than another according to the difference of their merits. But the souls of those who depart this life in actual mortal sin, or in original sin alone, go down…

question: Does the Roman pontiff rank first among the patriarchs, with Constantinople second, then Alexandria, Antioch, and Jerusalem?
catholic_answer: Yes. The Roman pontiff ranks first among the patriarchs, then Constantinople, Alexandria, Antioch, and Jerusalem, without prejudice to their privileges.
breakaway_answer: No as a claim of supreme jurisdiction. A primacy of honor among equals may be granted to Rome; first place with power over the whole Church is rejected.
passage_excerpt: Also, renewing the order of the other patriarchs which has been handed down in the canons, the patriarch of Constantinople should be second after the most holy Roman pontiff, third should be the patriarch of Alexandria, fourth the patriarch of Antioch, and fifth the patriarch of Jerusalem, without prejudice to all their privileges and rights.

question: Does the Holy Spirit proceed eternally from the Father and the Son as from one principle and a single spiration?
catholic_answer: Yes. The Holy Spirit proceeds eternally from the Father and the Son as from one principle and a single spiration, having his being from both.
breakaway_answer: No. The Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father alone as cause. Eternal procession from Father and Son as from one principle is rejected.
passage_excerpt: In the name of the holy Trinity, Father, Son and holy Spirit, we define, with the approval of this holy universal council of Florence, that the following truth of faith shall be believed and accepted by all Christians and thus shall all profess it: that the holy Spirit is eternally from the Father and the Son, and has his essence and his subsistent being from the Father together with the Son, and proceeds from both eternally as from one principle and a single spiration. We declare that when…

question: Because the Father gave the Son everything except being the Father, does the Son also have it from the Father that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son?
catholic_answer: Yes. Because the Father gave the Son everything except being the Father, the Son also eternally has it that the Spirit proceeds from the Son.
breakaway_answer: No. That inference does not hold. What the Son receives in being begotten does not include causing the Spirit’s procession; the Spirit proceeds from the Father.
passage_excerpt: And since the Father gave to his only-begotten Son in begetting him everything the Father has, except to be the Father, so the Son has eternally from the Father, by whom he was eternally begotten, this also, namely that the holy Spirit proceeds from the Son.

question: Was it licit to add the explanation 'and from the Son' (Filioque) to the Creed for the sake of declaring the truth?
catholic_answer: Yes. Adding ‘and from the Son’ to the Creed was licit and reasonable, under urgent necessity, to declare the truth of the Spirit’s procession.
breakaway_answer: No. The Creed must not be altered by that insertion. The faith is confessed with the older wording; adding the phrase was not licit.
passage_excerpt: We define also that the explanation of those words “and from the Son” was licitly and reasonably added to the creed for the sake of declaring the truth and from imminent need.

question: Is the Holy Spirit true God, proceeding from the Father and the Son?
catholic_answer: Yes. The Holy Spirit is true God, coequal and consubstantial with the Father and the Son, proceeding from the Father and the Son.
breakaway_answer: The Holy Spirit is true God, coequal with the Father and the Son, but proceeds from the Father—not from the Father and the Son.
canonical_citation: Lyons II, Profession of Faith of Michael Palaeologus (Denzinger 463)
passage_excerpt: He will come to judge the living and the dead, and will return to each one according to his works whether they were good or evil. We believe also that the Holy Spirit is complete and perfect and true God, proceeding from the Father and the Son, coequal and consubstantial, co-omnipotent, and coeternal through all things with the Father and the Son. We believe that this holy Trinity is not three Gods but one God, omnipotent, eternal, invisible, and unchangeable.

question: If the baptized die truly repentant before making full satisfaction, are their souls cleansed after death by purifying punishments, helped by Masses, prayers, and alms?
catholic_answer: Yes. Such souls are cleansed after death by purifying punishments, and the offerings of the living—Masses, prayers, and alms—relieve those pains.
breakaway_answer: No. There is no such state of purifying punishments after death relieved by Masses. The dead are commemorated and prayed for, but not under that purgatorial doctrine.
canonical_citation: Lyons II, Profession of Faith of Michael Palaeologus (Denzinger 464)
passage_excerpt: We believe that the true Church is holy, Catholic, apostolic, and one, in which is given one holy baptism and true remission of all sins. We believe also in the true resurrection of this flesh, which now we bear, and in eternal life. We believe also that the one author of the New and the Old Testament, of the Law, and of the Prophets and the Apostles is the omnipotent God and Lord.

question: Does the Roman Church rightly teach seven sacraments and prepare the Eucharist from unleavened bread, with the bread changed into Christ’s body and the wine into his blood?
catholic_answer: Yes. There are seven sacraments, and the Eucharist is prepared from unleavened bread, the bread changed into Christ’s body and the wine into his blood.
breakaway_answer: Seven mysteries may be honored in another sense, but unleavened bread is not the norm—leavened bread is used. That Latin sacramental package is not binding as a condition of faith.
canonical_citation: Lyons II, Profession of Faith of Michael Palaeologus (Denzinger 465)
passage_excerpt: The same holy Roman Church also holds and teaches that the ecclesiastical sacraments are seven: namely, one is baptism, concerning which we have spoken above; another is the sacrament of confirmation which the bishops confer through the imposition of hands when anointing the reborn; another is penance; another the Eucharist; another the sacrament of orders; another is matrimony; another extreme unction, which according to the doctrine of St. James is given to the sick. The same Roman Church…

question: Does the Roman Church hold the highest and complete primacy and spiritual power over the universal Catholic Church, received in Peter by the Roman pontiff?
catholic_answer: Yes. The highest and complete primacy and spiritual power over the universal Church belongs to that see in Peter’s successor, received from the Lord with fullness of power.
breakaway_answer: No. That see does not hold universal supremacy. Primacy, if any, is honor among sister churches, not complete spiritual power over the whole Church.
canonical_citation: Lyons II, Profession of Faith of Michael Palaeologus (Denzinger 466)
passage_excerpt: Also this same holy Roman Church holds the highest and complete primacy and spiritual power over the universal Catholic Church which she truly and humbly recognizes herself to have received with fullness of power from the Lord Himself in Blessed Peter, the chief or head of the Apostles whose successor is the Roman Pontiff. And just as to defend the truth of Faith she is held before all other things, so if any questions shall arise regarding faith they ought to be defined by her judgment. And…

question: Must everyone who raises a heresy against the Catholic faith as there explained be excommunicated and anathematized as a heretic under that regime?
catholic_answer: Yes. Every heresy raised against that faith is excommunicated and anathematized; those condemned are handed over for due punishment, clerics being first degraded from their orders.
breakaway_answer: No. Lay preaching and apostolic poverty outside that episcopal license are not condemned heresy under that regime; the anathematizing of such dissenters is refused.
passage_excerpt: We excommunicate and anathematize every heresy that raises against the holy, orthodox and Catholic faith which we have above explained; condemning all heretics under whatever names they may be known, for while they have different faces they are nevertheless bound to each other by their tails, since in all of them vanity is a common element. Those condemned, being handed over to the secular rulers of their bailiffs, let them be abandoned, to be punished with due justice, clerics being first…

question: After consecration, does the host remain true bread in nature while being Christ’s body only figuratively (remanence)?
catholic_answer: No. After consecration the host does not remain true bread in substance. The whole substance is converted; Christ’s body is truly present, not only figuratively.
breakaway_answer: Yes. After consecration the host remains true bread in nature while being Christ’s body figuratively—or in figure—so remanence is affirmed.
canonical_citation: Constance S15 [Articles of John Wyclif selected from the 260]
passage_excerpt: 1. Just as Christ is God and man at the same time, so the consecrated host is at the same time the body of Christ and true bread. For it is Christ’s body at least in figure and true bread in nature; or, which comes to the same thing, it is true bread naturally and Christ’s body figuratively.

question: Was John Wyclif rightly judged a heretic whose memory and teaching are to be condemned?
catholic_answer: Yes. He was rightly judged a heretic whose memory and teaching are to be condemned; the process found no lawful defender.
breakaway_answer: No. He was not a heretic. His memory and teaching should be honored as gospel reform, not condemned.
canonical_citation: Constance S8 [The council pronounces John Wyclif a heretic, condemns his memory and orders his bones to be exhumed]
passage_excerpt: Furthermore, a process was begun, on the authority or by decree of the Roman council, and at the command of the church and of the apostolic see, after a due interval of time, for the condemnation of the said Wyclif and his memory. Invitations and proclamations were issued summoning those who wished to defend him and his memory, if any still existed. However, nobody appeared who was willing to defend him or his memory.

question: Must the Christian people receive the Eucharist under both bread and wine, so that the laity communicate under the wine as well?
catholic_answer: No. The approved custom of communion under one kind for the laity stands; the people are not bound to receive under both kinds.
breakaway_answer: Yes. The sacrament should be given to the people under both kinds; withholding the cup from the laity is refused.
canonical_citation: Constance S13 [Condemnation of communion under both kinds, recently revived among the Bohemians by Jakoubek of Stribro]
passage_excerpt: In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Father and Son and holy Spirit, Amen. Certain people, in some parts of the world, have rashly dared to assert that the christian people ought to receive the holy sacrament of the eucharist under the forms of both bread and wine. They communicate the laity everywhere not only under the form of bread but also under that of wine, and they stubbornly assert that they should communicate even after a meal, or else without the need of a fast, contrary to…

question: Is the one holy universal church identical with the total number of those predestined to salvation?
catholic_answer: No. The one holy universal church is not simply identical with the set of the predestined. The visible Church is the communion of the baptized under rightful pastors, not that number alone.
breakaway_answer: Yes. The one holy universal church is precisely the total number of those predestined to salvation—that is what ‘church’ means.
canonical_citation: Constance S15 [Condemned articles of J. Hus]
passage_excerpt: 1. There is only one holy universal church, which is the total number of those predestined to salvation. It therefore follows that the universal holy church is only one, inasmuch as there is only one number of all those who are predestined to salvation.

question: Was John Hus rightly condemned by Constance as a heretic for obstinately holding Wycliffite and related errors?
catholic_answer: Yes. He was rightly condemned as a heretic for obstinately holding those errors against the faith.
breakaway_answer: No. He was not rightly condemned. The sentence was unjust; he is to be honored as a faithful witness, not a heretic.
passage_excerpt: The most holy general council of Constance, divinely assembled and representing the catholic church, for an everlasting record. Since a bad tree is wont to bear bad fruit, as truth itself testifies, so it is that John Wyclif, of cursed memory, by his deadly teaching, like a poisonous root, has brought forth many noxious sons, not in Christ Jesus through the gospel, as once the holy fathers brought forth faithful sons, but rather contrary to the saving faith of Christ, and he has left these…

question: Was Jerome of Prague rightly condemned by Constance as a heretic?
catholic_answer: Yes. He was rightly condemned as a heretic for not abiding in the faith as judged in that inquiry.
breakaway_answer: No. He was not rightly condemned. He is to be honored among the faithful reformers and martyrs, not as a heretic.
canonical_citation: Constance S21 [Sentence condemning Jerome of Prague]
passage_excerpt: In the name of the Lord, Amen. Christ our God and saviour, the true vine whose Father is the vine-dresser, said when teaching his disciples and other followers in these matters: If anyone does not abide in me, he shall be cast forth as a branch and shall wither. This holy synod of Constance is following the teaching and carrying out the commands of this sovereign teacher and master in this case of inquiry into heresy which was started by the same holy synod.

question: In the Eucharist, is the whole substance of bread and wine converted into Christ’s body and blood, with only the appearances remaining (transubstantiation)?
catholic_answer: Yes. The whole substance of bread and wine is converted into Christ’s body and blood; only the appearances remain—that conversion is rightly called transubstantiation.
breakaway_answer: No. There is no such conversion of the whole substance. Christ is present spiritually or sacramentally, or the elements remain bread and wine while signifying or conveying his body and blood.
notes: Umbrella label: concrete Protestant confessions vary; answer states the Reformational position Trent is targeting. Primary Trent interlocutor; Reformed/Anglican/Anabaptist often share the rejection.
passage_excerpt: CANON lI.-If any one saith, that, in the sacred and holy sacrament of the Eucharist, the substance of the bread and wine remains conjointly with the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, and denieth that wonderful and singular conversion of the whole substance of the bread into the Body, and of the whole substance of the wine into the Blood-the species Only of the bread and wine remaining-which conversion indeed the Catholic Church most aptly calls Transubstantiation; let him be anathema.

question: For the entire remission of sins in the sacrament of Penance, are contrition, confession, and satisfaction required as its three parts?
catholic_answer: Yes. Contrition, confession, and satisfaction are required as the three parts—as it were the matter—of that sacrament for the entire remission of sins.
breakaway_answer: No. Remission is not tied to those three acts as mandatory matter. Forgiveness comes by repentance and faith, without requiring auricular confession and satisfaction in that juridical form.

question: Did Christ institute the Sacrifice of the Mass as a true sacrifice of his body and blood?
catholic_answer: Yes. Christ instituted the Sacrifice of the Mass as a true sacrifice of his body and blood, a visible sacrifice representing and continuing the sacrifice of the cross.
breakaway_answer: No. Christ did not institute a propitiatory Mass-sacrifice. He instituted the Lord’s Supper as communion and remembrance of his once-for-all death, not a repeated sacrificial offering.
notes: Umbrella label: concrete Protestant confessions vary; answer states the Reformational position Trent is targeting. Primary Trent interlocutor; Reformed/Anglican/Anabaptist often share the rejection.

Forasmuch as, under the former Testament, according to the testimony of the Apostle Paul, there was no perfection, because of the weakness of the Levitical priesthood; there was need, God, the Father of mercies, so ordaining, that another priest should rise, according to the order of Melchisedech, our Lord Jesus Christ, who might consummate, and lead to what is perfect, as many as were to be sanctified.

question: Is the Sacrifice of the Mass truly propitiatory for both the living and the dead?
catholic_answer: Yes. In the Mass the same Christ is contained and immolated in an unbloody manner; the sacrifice is truly propitiatory for the living and the dead.
breakaway_answer: No. The Mass is not a propitiatory sacrifice for the living and the dead. Christ’s sacrifice on the cross was once for all; the Supper does not re-offer him for sin.

And forasmuch as, in this divine sacrifice which is celebrated in the mass, that same Christ is contained and immolated in an unbloody manner, who once offered Himself in a bloody manner on the altar of the cross; the holy Synod teaches, that this sacrifice is truly propritiatory and that by means thereof this is effected, that we obtain mercy, and find grace in seasonable aid, if we draw nigh unto…

question: May Masses be offered in honor of the saints?
catholic_answer: Yes. Masses may be offered in honor of the saints to obtain their intercession, while the sacrifice itself is offered to God alone.
breakaway_answer: No. Masses should not be offered in honor of the saints. Worship and sacrificial offering belong to God alone; the saints are not to be honored that way in the Supper.

question: Is the Canon of the Mass free from error and rightly retained as the Church’s holy prayer for offering the sacrifice?
catholic_answer: Yes. The Canon of the Mass is free from error—drawn from the Lord’s words and apostolic piety—and is rightly retained for offering the sacrifice.
breakaway_answer: No. That Canon is not free from error as a sacrificial prayer and should not be retained. The Supper should use a rite without that propitiatory canon.

question: Has the Church rightly instituted solemn Mass ceremonies—lights, incense, vestments, and varied tones of voice—as helps to divine worship?
catholic_answer: Yes. Lights, incense, vestments, and varied tones of voice are rightly instituted so that human minds may be raised to divine things.
breakaway_answer: No. Those ceremonies are not apostolic necessities. Ritual may be simplified or stripped; such externals are human tradition, not required helps to true worship.

And whereas such is the nature of man, that, without external helps, he cannot easily be raised to the meditation of divine things; therefore has holy Mother Church instituted certain rites, to wit that certain things be pronounced in the mass in a low, and others in a louder, tone.

question: Are Masses in which the priest alone communicates sacramentally lawful and to be approved?
catholic_answer: Yes. Masses in which the priest alone communicates are lawful and approved; they remain true sacrifices even when the faithful do not communicate sacramentally.
breakaway_answer: No. Private Masses of that kind are not lawful. The Lord’s Supper is a communion of the faithful; a priest communicating alone is not the Supper Christ instituted.

question: Must water be mixed with the wine in the chalice at Mass?
catholic_answer: Yes. Water must be mixed with the wine in the chalice, recalling Christ’s practice and the blood and water from his side, and the union of the people with him.
breakaway_answer: No. Mixing water with the wine is not required by Christ or necessary to the sacrament. Wine alone suffices; that mixture is a human ceremony.

question: Does the Church forbid celebrating the Mass everywhere in the vernacular, while requiring that its mysteries be explained to the people?
catholic_answer: Yes. It is not expedient that the Mass be celebrated everywhere in the vernacular, yet pastors must frequently explain its mysteries to the people.
breakaway_answer: No. The vernacular should not be restricted that way. The Lord’s Supper ought to be in a language the people understand, so they can hear and take part.

question: Is there in the New Testament a visible priesthood with power to consecrate and offer Christ’s body and blood and to forgive and retain sins?
catholic_answer: Yes. There is a visible New Testament priesthood with power to consecrate and offer Christ’s body and blood and to forgive and retain sins—not a mere office of preaching.
breakaway_answer: No. There is no sacrificing ministerial priesthood of that kind. Ministry is chiefly preaching the gospel, and all believers share a priesthood; consecrating sacrifice is rejected.
notes: Umbrella label: concrete Protestant confessions vary; answer states the Reformational position Trent is targeting. Primary Trent interlocutor; Reformed/Anglican/Anabaptist often share the rejection.
passage_excerpt: CANON I.--If any one saith, that there is not in the New Testament a visible and external priesthood; or that there is not any power of consecrating and offering the true body and blood of the Lord, and of forgiving and retaining sins; but only an office and bare ministry of preaching the Gospel, or, that those who do not preach are not priests at all; let him be anathema.

question: Is matrimony truly and properly one of the seven sacraments of the New Law, instituted by Christ and conferring grace?
catholic_answer: Yes. Matrimony is truly and properly one of the seven sacraments of the evangelic law, instituted by Christ and conferring grace.
breakaway_answer: No. Matrimony is an honorable estate, but it is not a sacrament of the New Law conferring grace in that sevenfold list.
notes: Umbrella label: concrete Protestant confessions vary; answer states the Reformational position Trent is targeting. Primary Trent interlocutor; Reformed/Anglican/Anabaptist often share the rejection.

question: Has the Church erred in teaching that the marriage bond cannot be dissolved by adultery and that neither party may marry another during the other’s life?
catholic_answer: No. The Church has not erred. The marriage bond cannot be dissolved by adultery, and neither spouse may marry another during the other’s lifetime.
breakaway_answer: Yes. The Church has erred on that point. For adultery or similar cause the bond may be treated as ended, and remarriage may be allowed while the other party still lives.

question: Did Christ grant the Church power to confer indulgences, and should that power be used?
catholic_answer: Yes. Christ granted the Church power to confer indulgences, she has used it from ancient times, and that power should continue to be used.
breakaway_answer: No. Christ did not grant a power to confer indulgences, and they should not be used. Remission of temporal penalty by that system has no place in the gospel.

question: Is there a purgatory, and can the souls detained there be helped by the suffrages of the faithful?
catholic_answer: Yes. There is a purgatory, and souls detained there are helped by the suffrages of the faithful, especially the sacrifice of the altar.
breakaway_answer: No. There is no purgatory as a post-mortem purifying state. The faithful departed are with Christ or await judgment without that intermediate purifying detention helped by Masses.

question: Should the faithful invoke the saints, venerate their relics, and honor sacred images?
catholic_answer: Yes. The faithful should invoke the saints, venerate their relics, and honor sacred images as helps to devotion toward God.
breakaway_answer: No. The faithful should not invoke the saints, venerate relics, or honor sacred images. Prayer is directed to God alone; such practices are rejected as unbiblical.

question: Has the Church authoritatively fixed the canon of Scripture, including the deuterocanonical books, and must sacred tradition be received with Scripture?
catholic_answer: Yes. The canon is authoritatively fixed, including the deuterocanonical books, and apostolic traditions concerning faith and morals are to be received with equal reverence alongside Scripture.
breakaway_answer: No. Scripture alone is the final rule. That closed canon—especially the deuterocanonicals as equal Scripture—is not binding, and tradition does not stand with equal authority beside Scripture.
notes: Umbrella label: concrete Protestant confessions vary; answer states the Reformational position Trent is targeting. Primary Trent interlocutor; Reformed/Anglican/Anabaptist often share the rejection.

passage_excerpt: The sacred and holy, ecumenical, and general Synod of Trent,--lawfully assembled in the Holy Ghost, the Same three legates of the Apostolic Sec presiding therein,--keeping this always in view, that, errors being removed, the purity itself of the Gospel be preserved in the Church; which (Gospel), before promised through the prophets in the holy Scriptures, our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, first promulgated with His own mouth, and then commanded to be preached by His Apostles to every…

question: After justification, can a debt of temporal punishment remain to be paid in this world or in Purgatory, even when guilt and eternal punishment are remitted?
catholic_answer: Yes. Guilt and eternal punishment may be remitted while a debt of temporal punishment still remains to be paid in this world or in Purgatory.
breakaway_answer: No. When justification remits guilt, no such remaining temporal debt in Purgatory is taught; Christ’s satisfaction covers the sinner without that residual penalty scheme.
notes: Umbrella label: concrete Protestant confessions vary; answer states the Reformational position Trent is targeting. Primary Trent interlocutor; Reformed/Anglican/Anabaptist often share the rejection.
passage_excerpt: CANON XXX.-If any one saith, that, after the grace of Justification has been received, to every penitent sinner the guilt is remitted, and the debt of eternal punishment is blotted out in such wise, that there remains not any debt of temporal punishment to be discharged either in this world, or in the next in Purgatory, before the entrance to the kingdom of heaven can be opened (to him); let him be anathema.

question: In coming to justification, does the human free will cooperate by assenting to God’s call, rather than remaining wholly passive?
catholic_answer: Yes. When God moves and calls, free will can and does cooperate by assenting, and can refuse; it is not merely passive like an inanimate thing.
breakaway_answer: No. In receiving justifying grace the will is passive, or does not synergistically cooperate. Justification is by grace through faith without that preparatory cooperation.
notes: Umbrella label: concrete Protestant confessions vary; answer states the Reformational position Trent is targeting. Primary Trent interlocutor; Reformed/Anglican/Anabaptist often share the rejection.
passage_excerpt: CANON IV.-If any one saith, that man's free will moved and excited by God, by assenting to God exciting and calling, nowise co-operates towards disposing and preparing itself for obtaining the grace of Justification; that it cannot refuse its consent, if it would, but that, as something inanimate, it does nothing whatever and is merely passive; let him be anathema.

question: Did Christ institute exactly seven sacraments—Baptism, Confirmation, Eucharist, Penance, Extreme Unction, Order, and Matrimony?
catholic_answer: Yes. Christ instituted exactly seven sacraments—Baptism, Confirmation, Eucharist, Penance, Extreme Unction, Order, and Matrimony—each truly and properly a sacrament.
breakaway_answer: No. Christ did not institute exactly those seven. In the strict sense there are two—baptism and the Lord’s Supper—though other rites may be valued without being sacraments of that kind.
notes: Umbrella label: concrete Protestant confessions vary; answer states the Reformational position Trent is targeting. Primary Trent interlocutor; Reformed/Anglican/Anabaptist often share the rejection.
canonical_citation: Trent S7 Sacraments in General canon 1
passage_excerpt: CANON I.-If any one saith, that the sacraments of the New Law were not all instituted by Jesus Christ, our Lord; or, that they are more, or less, than seven, to wit, Baptism, Confirmation, the Eucharist, Penance, Extreme Unction, Order, and Matrimony; or even that any one of these seven is not truly and properly a sacrament; let him be anathema.

question: Do all Christians have power to administer the word and all the sacraments?
catholic_answer: No. Not all Christians have power to administer the word and all the sacraments. That power belongs to those rightly ordained for the ministry.
breakaway_answer: Yes. All Christians share a priesthood of believers with broad power to minister the word and sacraments; ministry is not reserved to a sacrificing hierarchy.
notes: Umbrella label: concrete Protestant confessions vary; answer states the Reformational position Trent is targeting. Primary Trent interlocutor; Reformed/Anglican/Anabaptist often share the rejection.
canonical_citation: Trent S7 Sacraments in General canon 10
passage_excerpt: CANON X.-If any one saith, that all Christians have power to administer the word, and all the sacraments; let him be anathema.

question: When ministers confer the sacraments, must they intend at least to do what the Church does?
catholic_answer: Yes. When ministers confer the sacraments they must intend at least to do what the Church does; without that intention the sacrament is not effected.
breakaway_answer: No. Validity is not bound to that intention rule. What makes the rite effective is not dependence on intending ‘what the Church does’ in that sense.
notes: Umbrella label: concrete Protestant confessions vary; answer states the Reformational position Trent is targeting. Primary Trent interlocutor; Reformed/Anglican/Anabaptist often share the rejection.
canonical_citation: Trent S7 Sacraments in General canon 11
passage_excerpt: CANON XI.-If any one saith, that, in ministers, when they effect, and confer the sacraments, there is not required the intention at least of doing what the Church does; let him be anathema.

question: Is the impious justified by faith alone, such that nothing else is required to cooperate in obtaining the grace of justification, and no preparation of the will is necessary?
catholic_answer: No. Justification is not by faith alone in that sense; cooperation and a preparation and disposition of the will are required to obtain the grace of justification.
breakaway_answer: Yes. The impious is justified by faith alone; nothing else is required to cooperate in obtaining that grace, and the will’s preparatory works are not necessary in that sense.
notes: Umbrella label: concrete Protestant confessions vary; answer states the Reformational position Trent is targeting.
passage_excerpt: CANON IX.-If any one saith, that by faith alone the impious is justified; in such wise as to mean, that nothing else is required to co-operate in order to the obtaining the grace of Justification, and that it is not in any way necessary, that he be prepared and disposed by the movement of his own will; let him be anathema.

question: After baptism, are little children to be reckoned among the faithful even without actual faith of their own, so that omitting their baptism—or rebaptizing them later—is forbidden?
catholic_answer: Yes. Little children after baptism are reckoned among the faithful; they are not to be rebaptized when they reach discretion, and it is not better to omit their baptism for lack of their own act of faith.
breakaway_answer: No. Without their own actual faith, infants are not reckoned among the faithful by that baptism; believers’ baptism at years of discretion is required, and infant baptism is refused or redone.
notes: Umbrella label: concrete Protestant confessions vary; answer states the Reformational position Trent is targeting.
passage_excerpt: CANON XIII.-If any one saith, that little children, for that they have not actual faith, are not, after having received baptism, to be reckoned amongst the faithful; and that, for this cause, they are to be rebaptized when they have attained to years of discretion; or, that it is better that the baptism of such be omitted, than that, while not believing by their own act, they should be bapized in the faith alone of the Church; let him be anathema.

question: In the Eucharist, are the body and blood—together with the soul and divinity, and so the whole Christ—contained truly, really, and substantially, and not only as in a sign, figure, or virtue?
catholic_answer: Yes. The whole Christ is contained truly, really, and substantially in the sacrament—not only as in a sign, figure, or virtue.
breakaway_answer: No—not under that ‘truly, really, and substantially’ definition. Christ’s body is received in a heavenly and spiritual manner; the local substantial containment of that kind is refused.
notes: Umbrella label: concrete Protestant confessions vary; answer states the Reformational position Trent is targeting.
passage_excerpt: CANON I.-If any one denieth, that, in the sacrament of the most holy Eucharist, are contained truly, really, and substantially, the body and blood together with the soul and divinity of our Lord Jesus Christ, and consequently the whole Christ; but saith that He is only therein as in a sign, or in figure, or virtue; let him be anathema.

question: Is it by Christ’s own institution that Peter has perpetual successors in the primacy over the whole Church, and is the Roman pontiff that successor?
catholic_answer: Yes. By Christ’s own institution Peter has perpetual successors in the primacy over the whole Church, and the Roman pontiff is that successor by divine law.
breakaway_answer: No. Universal primacy of that kind is not by Christ’s institution. The Roman pontiff is not the perpetual successor of Peter over the whole Church in that sense; primacy is differently understood.
passage_excerpt: Therefore, if anyone says that it is not by the institution of Christ the lord himself (that is to say, by divine law) that blessed Peter should have perpetual successors in the primacy over the whole church; or that the Roman pontiff is not the successor of blessed Peter in this primacy: let him be anathema.

question: When the Roman pontiff speaks ex cathedra defining a doctrine of faith or morals to be held by the whole Church, does he possess infallible teaching authority?
catholic_answer: Yes. When the Roman pontiff speaks ex cathedra defining a doctrine of faith or morals to be held by the whole Church, he possesses that infallible teaching authority by the divine assistance promised in Peter.
breakaway_answer: No. He does not possess ex cathedra infallible authority from himself apart from the Church’s consent. Doctrinal definitions require the Church’s wider authority, not a personal infallible privilege of that kind.
passage_excerpt: Therefore, faithfully adhering to the tradition received from the beginning of the christian faith, to the glory of God our saviour, for the exaltation of the catholic religion and for the salvation of the christian people, with the approval of the sacred council, we teach and define as a divinely revealed dogma that when the Roman pontiff speaks EX CATHEDRA, that is, when, in the exercise of his office as shepherd and teacher of all Christians, in virtue of his supreme apostolic authority, he…

question: Must anyone who rejects the definition of the Roman pontiff’s infallible teaching authority be anathematized?
catholic_answer: Yes. Anyone who has the temerity to reject that definition of the Roman pontiff’s infallible teaching authority is anathematized.
breakaway_answer: No. That definition of infallible papal teaching authority is refused; rejecting it is not treated as anathema, because doctrinal definitions are not bound by that personal privilege.
passage_excerpt: So then, should anyone, which God forbid, have the temerity to reject this definition of ours: let him be anathema.

question: Does the Roman pontiff hold full and supreme ordinary jurisdiction over the whole Church in faith, morals, discipline, and government—not merely an office of supervision and guidance?
catholic_answer: Yes. He has the full and supreme power of jurisdiction over the whole Church in faith and morals and in discipline and government, ordinary and immediate over all churches and pastors.
breakaway_answer: No. He does not hold that full and supreme ordinary jurisdiction over the whole Church; national or independent Catholic structures govern without that absolute papal power.
passage_excerpt: So, then, if anyone says that the Roman pontiff has merely an office of supervision and guidance, and not the full and supreme power of jurisdiction over the whole church, and this not only in matters of faith and morals, but also in those which concern the discipline and government of the church dispersed throughout the whole world; or that he has only the principal part, but not the absolute fullness, of this supreme power; or that this power of his is not ordinary and immediate both over…

question: Was blessed Peter appointed by Christ as prince of the apostles and visible head of the whole Church militant, receiving a primacy of true jurisdiction and not of honor only?
catholic_answer: Yes. Peter was appointed prince of all the apostles and visible head of the whole Church militant, receiving a primacy of true and proper jurisdiction directly from Christ—not honor only.
breakaway_group: Mariavite Church (Old Catholic Church of the Mariavites)
breakaway_answer: No. That primacy of true jurisdiction over the whole militant Church is refused; a primacy of honor only, or a rejected papal claim, is taught instead.
passage_excerpt: Therefore, if anyone says that blessed Peter the apostle was not appointed by Christ the lord as prince of all the apostles and visible head of the whole church militant; or that it was a primacy of honour only and not one of true and proper jurisdiction that he directly and immediately received from our lord Jesus Christ himself: let him be anathema.
